content: Turn to long axis with the needle in plane and the whole shaft and tip are visible entering the vein. Harder to hold steady, but no guessing about depth.

where: Lines › Learn › Ultrasound-guided IJ: seeing the tip › The wrong vessel
content: Aim too medially and the needle finds the carotid. Do not trust colour — in shock and hypoxaemia arterial blood can look dark. A pulsatile flow and an arterial pressure on the transducer settle it. Remove the needle and compress.

where: Lines › Learn › Ultrasound-guided IJ: seeing the tip › When the vein lies on the artery
content: Turn the head too far and the vein rolls over the artery. A needle that goes through both walls of the vein arrives in the carotid. Keep the tip in view.

where: Lines › Learn › Ultrasound-guided IJ: seeing the tip › See the wire
content: Before any dilator: find the wire as a bright echo inside the vein, in short axis and again in long axis. Only then dilate — to the depth of the vessel, never beyond — and keep hold of the wire until the catheter is in.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › The term circulation
content: At term the heart pumps about forty percent more blood: a bigger stroke volume, and a heart rate fifteen beats faster. The placenta is a low resistance circuit and progesterone relaxes vessels, so diastolic pressure runs a little low. Her blood volume is about six and a half litres.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › Flat on her back
content: Lay her flat, and the heavy uterus compresses the inferior vena cava against the spine. Less blood returns to the heart, output falls by up to a third, and the pressure drops. The placenta cannot autoregulate, so the baby feels the fall first.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › Displace the uterus
content: Push the uterus up and to her left, or tilt her fifteen to thirty degrees, and venous return comes back within a minute. In a collapsed woman beyond about twenty weeks, this goes with the first compressions.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › A litre lost
content: After delivery she bleeds. A litre is only about fifteen percent of her expanded volume, so the pressure barely changes and the heart rate creeps up. The shock index, heart rate divided by systolic pressure, is already close to one.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › Nearly two litres
content: At nearly two litres she is compensating hard: a fast heart rate, a narrow pulse pressure, cool hands. The systolic pressure is still around ninety. Young pregnant women hold their pressure until very late; a shock index well above one tells the truth.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › Decompensation
content: Beyond about a third of her volume the vasoconstriction runs out, and the pressure falls fast. This is late. She needs blood, not more crystalloid, and the bleeding stopped.

where: Lines › Learn › The pregnant circulation: position and postpartum haemorrhage › Stop the bleeding, replace blood
content: Treat the cause and the volume together: uterine massage and uterotonic drugs for an atonic uterus, the commonest cause; tranexamic acid early; warmed blood and products; calcium; and early obstetric and anaesthetic help. Here, blood restores her output.

where: Lines › Learn › Shock in a child: the pressure is the last thing to go › A well four year old
content: A well four year old weighing sixteen kilos. The heart rate is about a hundred and the systolic pressure about ninety. Her whole blood volume is only about eighty millilitres per kilo, around one point three litres. A child’s small heart cannot raise its stroke volume much, so output depends on heart rate.

where: Lines › Learn › Shock in a child: the pressure is the last thing to go › Fifteen percent lost
content: She has lost about two hundred millilitres, fifteen percent of her volume. The heart rate climbs past the normal range, the pulse pressure narrows, and capillary refill slows. The blood pressure has not fallen at all.

where: Lines › Learn › Shock in a child: the pressure is the last thing to go › Compensated shock
content: At a quarter of her volume she is pale, mottled and tachycardic above one hundred and fifty, with a capillary refill of four seconds. Her systolic pressure is still normal. This is compensated shock, and it must be recognised now, from the heart rate and the skin.

where: Lines › Learn › Shock in a child: the pressure is the last thing to go › Decompensation
content: Beyond about a third, vasoconstriction can no longer hold the pressure, and it falls below seventy plus twice her age. Hypotension in a child is a late sign: she has lost nearly forty percent of her blood.

where: Lines › Learn › Shock in a child: the pressure is the last thing to go › Bradycardia: arrest is close
content: Now the heart rate falls. In a shocked child, bradycardia is not improvement: it means the heart is failing from lack of oxygen, and cardiac arrest is close.

where: Lines › Learn › Shock in a child: the pressure is the last thing to go › Blood, in small measured boluses
content: Treat with blood in boluses of about ten millilitres per kilo, reassessing heart rate, pressure and refill after each, while the bleeding is controlled. After two boluses her pressure and heart rate have recovered. Doses and volumes follow your paediatric protocol.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › Four inflows, one ring
content: Two internal carotids and two vertebral arteries feed the brain. At its base, the Circle of Willis links them, so flow can reroute around a blocked feeder.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › A clot in the left M1
content: A thrombus lodges in the left middle cerebral artery, beyond the circle. Nothing in the ring can bypass it. Flow past the clot stops.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › Core and penumbra
content: The deep territory, fed only by end arteries, dies within minutes. That is the core, in magenta. Around it, tissue fed thinly by collaterals from the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries is silent but alive. That is the penumbra, in amber.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › The penumbra shrinks with time
content: Hour by hour, penumbra converts to core. The lower the flow in a region, the sooner it infarcts.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › Collateral flow is pressure-passive
content: Ischaemic vessels have lost autoregulation, so collateral flow follows blood pressure. Let the mean arterial pressure fall to sixty and the core grows faster.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › Protect the pressure
content: Restore the pressure, and the penumbra holds on longer.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › Reopen the artery
content: Thrombectomy at four hours restores flow. The core that already died stays. Everything still in the penumbra is saved. That difference is the reason for speed.

where: Brain › Learn › Time is brain: a left M1 occlusion › Two patients, one clot
content: The same clot, a different outcome. The size of the final infarct is set by collaterals, blood pressure and, above all, time to reperfusion.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › 0 min · Onset
content: Minute zero. A clot blocks the left middle cerebral artery. Right-sided weakness and aphasia start at once.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › 0–45 min · Scene and transport
content: While the crew recognises a large-vessel stroke and transports, the core is already growing from the deep territory outward.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › 45–60 min · Door → non-contrast CT
content: At the hospital the first scan is a non-contrast CT, to exclude bleeding. There is no haemorrhage. Look for the hyperdense clot in the left middle cerebral artery, and subtle loss of grey–white differentiation in the deep grey matter.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › CT angiogram
content: The CT angiogram shows the cut-off: contrast stops at the clot, and the branches beyond fill only faintly, backwards, through collaterals.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › CT perfusion
content: Perfusion maps separate tissue that is already lost, with very low blood flow, from tissue that is only delayed. A large delayed area around a small core is a mismatch — salvageable brain.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › 72–150 min · Thrombectomy
content: The patient goes for thrombectomy. At two and a half hours from onset the clot is pulled out and flow returns.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › 24 h · Final infarct
content: A day later, the final infarct is the core that existed at reperfusion. Everything that was still penumbra has been saved.

where: Brain › Learn › Stroke time machine: onset to reperfusion › What every hour costs
content: Use the numbers under the images: the same patient, reopened an hour later, keeps a larger infarct. Minutes at every step — scene, door, scan, groin — become brain.

where: Brain › Learn › Large-vessel occlusion: recognise, confirm, decide › Cortical signs point to a large vessel
content: A left middle cerebral artery occlusion takes out the language cortex and the motor strip for face and arm. Expect aphasia, right-sided weakness worse in face and arm than leg, and the eyes deviated toward the left — toward the lesion.

where: Brain › Learn › Large-vessel occlusion: recognise, confirm, decide › The other side looks different
content: On the right, the same clot causes left-sided weakness with neglect: the patient ignores the left side of the world and may deny the weakness. Cortical signs like these, with a dense deficit, suggest a large vessel rather than a small lacune.

where: Brain › Learn › Large-vessel occlusion: recognise, confirm, decide › CTA confirms the target
content: Back to the left-sided stroke. The angiogram shows where contrast stops. That is the target for thrombectomy.

where: Brain › Learn › Large-vessel occlusion: recognise, confirm, decide › Poor collaterals: a fast progressor
content: With poor collaterals, almost the whole territory is already core by ninety minutes. The perfusion maps show little left to save.

where: Brain › Learn › Large-vessel occlusion: recognise, confirm, decide › Good collaterals: a slow progressor
content: With good collaterals, the same clot at the same time leaves a small core and a large penumbra. These patients can benefit even many hours later.

where: Brain › Learn › Large-vessel occlusion: recognise, confirm, decide › Transport decisions spend minutes
content: For a moderate-collateral patient, look at the final-core numbers: reopening now, in one hour, or in three hours. A detour to a hospital that cannot do thrombectomy usually costs that hour. That is why large-vessel screening in the field matters.

where: Brain › Learn › Intracerebral haemorrhage: the first hours › A bleed, not a clot
content: A hypertensive bleed in the left basal ganglia. On non-contrast CT fresh blood is bright. This is why every stroke gets a scan before any clot-dissolving drug.

where: Brain › Learn › Intracerebral haemorrhage: the first hours › Estimating the volume
content: Bedside volume estimate: multiply the largest diameter by the perpendicular diameter by the number of slices with blood, in centimetres, and halve it. Thirty millilitres is a common threshold for a worse outcome.

where: Brain › Learn › Intracerebral haemorrhage: the first hours › It grows — faster at high pressure
content: Many haematomas keep growing in the first few hours. With a systolic pressure near one hundred and ninety, watch the volume and the midline shift climb.

where: Brain › Learn › Intracerebral haemorrhage: the first hours › Lower the pressure early
content: Rewind and lower the systolic pressure to about one hundred and forty from the start. The same bleed grows less. Early, smooth pressure control and reversing any anticoagulant are the core of the first hour.

where: Brain › Learn › Intracerebral haemorrhage: the first hours › Mass effect
content: A growing clot pushes the midline across and raises intracranial pressure. Falling consciousness, a new blown pupil or vomiting means the mass effect is winning.

where: Brain › Learn › Subarachnoid haemorrhage and vasospasm › Blood in the cisterns
content: A ruptured aneurysm on the circle of Willis fills the basal cisterns and the Sylvian fissures with blood: the bright star shape around the circle on non-contrast CT. The story is a sudden, worst-ever headache.

where: Brain › Learn › Subarachnoid haemorrhage and vasospasm › Where aneurysms sit
content: Most aneurysms arise at branch points of the circle: the anterior communicating, the posterior communicating origin, and the middle cerebral bifurcation. Securing the aneurysm early prevents a re-bleed.

where: Brain › Learn › Subarachnoid haemorrhage and vasospasm › Days 3 to 14: vasospasm
content: Days later, blood breakdown products make the arteries around the circle constrict. Narrowed vessels on angiography, and delayed ischaemia in their territories: a new deficit or falling consciousness between day three and day fourteen.

where: Brain › Learn › Subarachnoid haemorrhage and vasospasm › Protecting the brain
content: Keep the patient euvolaemic, avoid hypotension, give nimodipine, and watch closely for a new deficit so spasm can be treated early.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › A closed box
content: The skull holds brain, blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Its volume is fixed, so anything new — a haematoma, swelling, trapped fluid — has to be paid for by pushing something else out.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Compensation
content: A twenty millilitre haematoma. Cerebrospinal fluid moves down into the spinal canal and venous blood leaves the skull. The pressure barely moves: this is the flat part of the curve.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Past the knee
content: At about fifty millilitres the buffers are used up. Every extra millilitre now raises the pressure steeply. The waveform shows it too: the second peak rises above the first as the brain stiffens.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Cerebral perfusion pressure
content: Blood reaches the brain at the mean arterial pressure minus the intracranial pressure. Let the blood pressure fall to a mean of seventy and the perfusion pressure drops toward forty: ischaemia without any blocked artery.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Uncal herniation
content: More volume, and the midline shifts. The medial temporal lobe is pushed over the tentorial edge and compresses the third nerve: the pupil on the side of the mass dilates and stops reacting, the opposite limbs weaken and consciousness falls.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › The Cushing response
content: When the brainstem itself is squeezed, the body drives the blood pressure up to keep perfusing it, the heart slows and breathing becomes irregular. This is late, and it means herniation is under way.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Buy time
content: Head up thirty degrees with the neck straight, so veins drain. Hyperosmolar therapy draws water out of the brain. A short period of lower carbon dioxide constricts the vessels — useful as a bridge, harmful if prolonged, because it cuts blood flow too.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Remove the volume
content: The definitive answer is to remove the volume or open the box: evacuate the clot, or take off a piece of skull. The curve flattens and the pupils recover if it is in time.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Hydrocephalus
content: A different cause: after subarachnoid haemorrhage, blood blocks the drainage of cerebrospinal fluid. The ventricles fill with fluid that is still being made and balloon on the scan, and the pressure rises without any midline shift.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › External ventricular drain
content: An external ventricular drain, zeroed at the tragus — level with the foramen of Monro. Open at fifteen centimetres of water, fluid drains whenever the pressure exceeds that height, and the pressure settles there.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Levelling errors
content: Raise the head of the bed without moving the chamber and the drain is now effectively fifteen centimetres too low. It overdrains: the ventricles collapse and bridging veins can tear. Re-level every time the patient or the bed moves.

where: Brain › Learn › ICP, herniation and the EVD › Clamped
content: Left clamped after a transfer, nothing drains and the pressure climbs back. Clamp only for the time the protocol allows, and read the pressure against the patient, not the clock.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › A loud murmur
content: A well child with a loud, harsh murmur at the lower left sternal border that lasts all through systole. The heart itself looks normal in size.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › The defect
content: Here is the cause: a small hole in the ventricular septum, just below the aortic valve.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › A big gradient makes a fast jet
content: In systole the left ventricle generates about one hundred and twenty millimetres of mercury, the right about twenty-five. Across a small hole that gradient drives a jet near five metres per second. On colour Doppler it aliases into a mosaic. Loud murmur, small shunt.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › A large defect: more flow, less noise
content: Now a large defect. Pressures on the two sides move closer, so the jet is slower and the murmur can be softer — yet far more blood crosses. Pulmonary flow is more than twice systemic flow.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › The lungs are flooded
content: The shunted blood goes straight out through the pulmonary artery. The lungs carry the extra flow at higher pressure: the infant breathes fast, sweats with feeds and fails to gain weight.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › The left heart takes the volume
content: All that extra pulmonary blood returns to the left atrium and left ventricle, which dilate. A VSD volume-loads the LEFT heart, even though the hole feeds the right ventricle.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › Years of overcirculation
content: Left unrepaired, years of high flow and pressure remodel the small pulmonary arteries and resistance climbs. Watch the right ventricle thicken, the gradient shrink, flow become bidirectional, and finally reverse: right to left.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › Eisenmenger syndrome
content: Now deoxygenated blood enters the aorta. The patient is cyanosed and clubbed, and the murmur has faded. At this stage closing the hole would remove the right ventricle’s only escape valve, so repair is no longer possible.

where: Heart › Learn › Ventricular septal defect: from murmur to Eisenmenger › Repair in time
content: Closed in infancy, before the pulmonary vessels remodel, the circulation returns to two separate circuits and the heart remodels back toward normal. Many small muscular defects close on their own.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › Before the first breath
content: Before birth the lungs are full of fluid and their vessels are tightly constricted, so pulmonary resistance is very high. The placenta, not the lungs, supplies oxygen. Blood from the right heart bypasses the lungs through the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › The first breaths
content: With the first breaths, air replaces lung fluid and oxygen relaxes the pulmonary vessels. Resistance falls steeply, pulmonary blood flow rises, and flow through the ductus turns around: now it runs from the aorta into the pulmonary artery.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › The first ten minutes
content: Saturation rises slowly after birth. A healthy baby may be only sixty to sixty five percent at one minute, and eighty to eighty five at five. Measure on the right hand or wrist, which is supplied before the ductus, and aim for the target band, not a hundred percent.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › The duct closes
content: Over hours to days the ductus constricts and closes, and the flap of the foramen ovale is held shut by the higher left atrial pressure. Two circuits now run in series, as in the adult.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › When resistance will not fall
content: In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, the pulmonary vessels stay constricted. Pulmonary pressure stays close to or above aortic pressure, and blood crosses the ductus from right to left, into the descending aorta. The right hand stays pink while the feet are blue: compare a pre-ductal and a post-ductal probe.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › A vicious circle
content: Hypoxia, acidosis, cold and a high carbon dioxide all constrict the pulmonary vessels further. More blood bypasses the lungs, the baby becomes more hypoxic and acidotic, and resistance climbs again.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › Breaking the circle
content: Treatment breaks the circle: oxygen, gentle ventilation to a normal carbon dioxide, warmth, correcting acidosis, surfactant where the lungs need it, and inhaled nitric oxide, which relaxes only the pulmonary vessels. As resistance falls, ductal flow turns left to right and the difference disappears.

where: Heart › Learn › Newborn transition and pulmonary hypertension (PPHN) › No difference is not reassurance
content: One trap. If the right heart struggles and right atrial pressure rises, blood also crosses the foramen ovale from right to left. Then the hand and the foot are both low, with no difference between them. A low pre-ductal saturation still needs an explanation.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Four places to look
content: Lying flat, free fluid in the abdomen runs to the lowest spaces: between the liver and the right kidney, around the spleen, and down into the pelvis. The FAST exam puts a probe over each of those, plus under the ribs to see the pericardium.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › A normal FAST
content: This is the same normal abdomen as ultrasound. Liver sits against kidney, spleen against kidney, the bladder is black because urine reflects no echoes, and the pericardium hugs the heart. No black stripe anywhere.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Too early to see
content: A liver laceration two minutes after the crash. Blood is already leaking, but a few tens of millilitres spread thinly and every window still looks negative. An early negative scan does not rule out injury: repeat it.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Morison’s pouch lights up first
content: A few minutes later a black stripe opens between liver and kidney. The hepatorenal space is the most dependent upper-abdominal space when supine, so the right upper quadrant is usually positive first.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › The same blood in 3D
content: In the anatomy the pool sits exactly where the probe was looking: tucked behind the liver, in front of the right kidney.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Spleen: look above it too
content: A grade four splenic injury. On the left, blood collects around the spleen and under the diaphragm before it reaches the kidney, so the left window must include the space above the spleen.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Minutes matter
content: Untreated, the bleed keeps going. Watch the left stripe widen, the right upper quadrant and then the pelvis fill, and the haemorrhage class climb in the side panel. Blood pressure holds until a third or more of the blood volume is gone.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › The bleed FAST cannot see
content: A different patient: an aneurysm has ruptured into the retroperitoneum, behind the lining of the abdomen. More than a litre is lost, yet not a drop is free in the peritoneal cavity.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Negative FAST, unstable patient
content: Every FAST window is negative. The clue is elsewhere: a wide aorta on the separate aortic view, back or flank pain, and shock with no free fluid. Pelvic fractures and kidney injuries bleed into the same hidden space.

where: Abdomen › Learn › FAST: where free blood goes — and what it misses › Reading a FAST
content: Positive in a shocked trauma patient: the abdomen is a likely source. Negative: not proof of safety — it may be early, the fluid may be retroperitoneal, or the view may be poor. Repeat it when the patient changes.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › A normal aorta
content: The abdominal aorta below the renal arteries is normally about two centimetres wide. An aneurysm is a permanent widening to three centimetres or more.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › Growing
content: Aneurysms grow slowly, often silently. Wall tension rises with radius, so the wider it gets the faster it tends to grow and the higher the rupture risk; above about five and a half centimetres repair usually outweighs the risk of waiting.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › On ultrasound
content: A transverse bedside scan measures it outer wall to outer wall. Much of the sac is lined with grey thrombus; the flowing lumen is the smaller black circle inside.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › Contained rupture
content: Sudden back or flank pain and a faint. The sac has torn at the back, into the retroperitoneum, where the surrounding tissue can tamponade it for a while.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › Deceptively stable
content: The haematoma grows behind the peritoneum. Heart rate climbs while pressure is still near normal. This window is the chance to get the patient to repair.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › FAST stays negative
content: The FAST windows are black-stripe free, because none of this blood is intraperitoneal. The aortic view shows the wide sac with a dark cuff of haematoma beside it.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › Free rupture
content: If the tear opens into the peritoneal cavity there is nothing left to contain it. Within minutes every FAST window fills and the patient moves to class four haemorrhage.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Abdominal aortic aneurysm: intact, contained, free rupture › What changes outcome
content: Outcome depends on control of the aorta, in the operating theatre or the endovascular suite. Many teams accept a lower blood pressure while the patient stays conscious, to avoid pushing more blood out of the hole before it is controlled.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › A tearing pain
content: Sudden, severe, tearing pain between the shoulder blades. Hypertensive and tachycardic. A pressure difference between the arms, or a pulse deficit, raises the suspicion. The test is a CT angiogram from the chest to the groins.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Type A: the ascending aorta
content: At the level of the pulmonary artery, look first at the ascending aorta in front. A flap here is Stanford type A: it can tear into the pericardium, the coronaries or the aortic valve. That is a surgical emergency.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Type B: descending only
content: In this patient the ascending aorta is clean and round. The flap is only in the descending aorta, beside the spine: Stanford type B. Most are managed medically unless they are complicated.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › True and false lumen
content: Follow it down. The flap divides the aorta into two channels. The true lumen is usually the smaller, denser one; the false lumen is larger and fills more slowly. Which lumen feeds each branch matters.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Malperfusion
content: Compare the kidneys. The left one barely enhances: its artery arises from a false lumen that is not delivering blood. Malperfusion of a kidney, the bowel or a leg turns an uncomplicated type B into a complicated one.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Into the iliacs
content: The flap continues into the left common iliac artery. Check the leg pulses and the groin: a cold, pulseless leg is another malperfusion sign.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Rate first
content: Treatment starts with impulse control. A short-acting beta-blocker brings the heart rate to about sixty, reducing the force of each ejection on the torn wall. Watch the rate fall while the pressure is still high.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Then the pressure
content: Only then add a vasodilator to bring the systolic pressure below about one hundred and twenty, as far as perfusion allows: urine output, mental state and the malperfused organs set the floor.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Why not the vasodilator first
content: Give the vasodilator alone and the baroreflex answers with tachycardia and a harder, faster ejection — more shear on the flap. Beta-blockade before vasodilation.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Aortic dissection: type, extent, malperfusion, anti-impulse › Who needs what
content: Type A: control the pressure and get to cardiac surgery. Type B with rupture, malperfusion or uncontrollable pain: endovascular repair. Uncomplicated type B: impulse control, monitoring and repeat imaging.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Spleen and liver injury: the response to blood decides › Low grade, stable
content: A grade two splenic laceration an hour after a fall. There is blood around the spleen and the FAST is positive, but the heart rate and pressure are normal and the bleeding has slowed. Stable patients like this usually get a CT and are managed without an operation, with close observation.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Spleen and liver injury: the response to blood decides › High grade
content: A grade four injury bleeds faster. Thirty minutes in, three FAST windows are positive and she is in class two shock: the heart rate is up, the pressure still normal.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Spleen and liver injury: the response to blood decides › Give blood, and watch
content: A litre of blood restores her circulating volume and the heart rate settles, for now. The blood already in the abdomen stays there. How she responds over the next half hour sorts patients into three groups.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Spleen and liver injury: the response to blood decides › A transient responder
content: Forty five minutes later she has bled the transfused blood away and the class is climbing again. A transient responder is still bleeding: she needs haemorrhage control, by angioembolisation if it is immediately available and she is safe to go there, otherwise the operating room.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Spleen and liver injury: the response to blood decides › A non-responder
content: A grade five liver injury. An hour and a half in, a litre of blood has made no difference: she is in class three shock. No response means an operation now, with damage control surgery, packing and a massive transfusion protocol.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Spleen and liver injury: the response to blood decides › Control stops the clock
content: Once the bleeding is controlled, the loss stops growing. The fluid in the abdomen is still there on ultrasound, but transfusion can finally catch up, and the haemorrhage class falls.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion › Pain out of proportion
content: A seventy eight year old with atrial fibrillation and sudden, severe central abdominal pain. The abdomen is soft and hardly tender. Pain out of proportion to the examination is the classic early sign, and the bowel still looks normal.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion › An embolus in the artery
content: A clot from the fibrillating left atrium has lodged in the superior mesenteric artery, which supplies most of the small bowel. On the CT angiogram the artery, just in front of the aorta, does not fill with contrast.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion › The wall stops enhancing
content: Hours later the small bowel wall stops enhancing. Early in the course the lactate can still be normal, so a normal lactate does not rule this out.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion › Infarction
content: Once the bowel infarcts it turns dusky, gas appears in its wall, the lining sloughs, and bacteria and toxins reach the blood. Peritonitis, acidosis and shock follow, and the abdomen finally becomes tender.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Acute mesenteric ischaemia: pain out of proportion › The CT at infarction
content: On CT, gas now lies in the bowel wall. The treatment is time: urgent revascularisation, by embolectomy or an endovascular route, resection of dead bowel, fluids, antibiotics and anticoagulation. Every hour of delay costs bowel.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Bowel obstruction and perforation › Small-bowel obstruction
content: Small bowel obstruction, most often from adhesions after previous surgery, or a hernia. Above the block the bowel dilates with fluid and gas, she vomits, and the abdomen distends.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Bowel obstruction and perforation › On CT
content: On CT the loops are wide and full of fluid, with gas floating on top: air fluid levels. Surgeons look for the transition point, where dilated bowel meets collapsed bowel, and for signs that the blood supply is failing.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Bowel obstruction and perforation › Where the fluid goes
content: Litres of fluid are trapped in the bowel wall and lumen, or lost as vomit. She becomes dry, with a rising heart rate and falling urine output. Decompress with a nasogastric tube, replace the fluid, and watch for strangulation.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Bowel obstruction and perforation › Perforation
content: Perforation: a hole in the gut lets air and bowel content into the peritoneum. Lying flat, the air rises to the front of the abdomen; sitting up, it collects under the diaphragm.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Bowel obstruction and perforation › Free air on ultrasound
content: On ultrasound, free air makes a bright line with reverberations that hides what lies behind it, over the liver in the upper abdomen. The fluid in these windows is not blood but gut content, so a positive scan here means peritonitis, not haemorrhage.

where: Abdomen › Learn › Bowel obstruction and perforation › Free air on CT
content: On CT the air sits in front of the liver and bowel, outside the gut. Perforation with peritonitis needs resuscitation, antibiotics and an operation.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Negative FAST, left-sided impact (Novice)
item: The first scan: what does it tell you?
content: Story: Motorcyclist, left lower rib fractures, minutes after the crash. You scan all four windows in the aircraft. Then you scan again ten minutes later. Answer: Not enough blood yet to see — a negative FAST does not exclude injury; repeat it. Other options: No intra-abdominal injury — the abdomen is cleared | The bleeding must be retroperitoneal | The probe must be in the wrong place. Explanation: FAST needs on the order of a few hundred mL of intraperitoneal fluid before a window turns positive. Early after injury it is often negative; its value is in repeating it as the picture evolves.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Negative FAST, left-sided impact (Novice)
item: Ten minutes later, where does blood from the spleen appear first?
content: Answer: LUQ — splenorenal space and above the spleen. Other options: RUQ — Morison’s pouch | Subxiphoid — pericardium | Nowhere until it reaches the pelvis. Explanation: Morison’s pouch is the most sensitive window overall, but splenic blood collects around the spleen and in the splenorenal space first, then spills down the left gutter to the pelvis before it reaches the right upper quadrant.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Positive FAST, rising heart rate (Intermediate)
content: Story: Same patient, now 30 minutes after the crash and still in the aircraft. Scan all four windows. Answer: RUQ, LUQ and pelvis. Other options: LUQ only | Pericardium only | None — it is retroperitoneal. Explanation: With several hundred mL the fluid has filled the left upper quadrant, run down the left paracolic gutter into the pelvis and reached Morison’s pouch.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Positive FAST, rising heart rate (Intermediate)
content: Answer: Class II — tachycardic, pressure still held. Other options: Class I | Class III | Class IV. Explanation: Blood loss of roughly 15–30 %: the heart rate climbs and the pulse pressure narrows, but systolic pressure is still maintained. Waiting for hypotension means waiting for class III.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Back pain, pulsatile mass, negative FAST (Advanced)
item: What does the CT show at the infrarenal level?
content: Story: 74-year-old, sudden back and left flank pain, near-syncope at home. The FAST is negative. The receiving centre sends the CT angiogram through before you land. Answer: A 7 cm aneurysm with a retroperitoneal haematoma — contained rupture. Other options: An intact aneurysm, no bleeding | Free intraperitoneal rupture | A dissection flap. Explanation: A large aneurysm with eccentric thrombus and blood beside it in the retroperitoneum: a contained rupture. It can become free rupture at any moment.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Back pain, pulsatile mass, negative FAST (Advanced)
content: Answer: FAST sees intraperitoneal fluid; this blood is retroperitoneal. Other options: The haematoma is too small to matter | The scan was done too early — repeat it to rule out rupture | Aneurysms cannot be seen on ultrasound. Explanation: The retroperitoneum is invisible to FAST. A negative FAST in a patient with a known or suspected AAA and pain does not rule out rupture.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Back pain, pulsatile mass, negative FAST (Advanced)
content: Answer: Permissive hypotension: enough pressure for mentation, no push to normal, straight to a vascular centre. Other options: Fluid bolus to a normal blood pressure | Start a vasodilator to protect the aneurysm | Divert to the nearest hospital for a formal CT first. Explanation: Raising the pressure can turn a contained rupture into a free one. Accept a low pressure while the patient is awake, give blood rather than crystalloid when needed, and get to definitive repair.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Tearing chest pain to the back (Advanced)
item: What type is this, and what does it need?
content: Story: 58-year-old with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. The CTA is on your screen at the chest level. Answer: Stanford type A — the ascending aorta is involved: emergency surgery. Other options: Stanford type B — medical therapy first | No dissection — the aorta is normal | Type B — immediate endovascular stent. Explanation: Any involvement of the ascending aorta makes it type A: at risk of tamponade, aortic regurgitation and coronary occlusion. It goes to cardiothoracic surgery.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Tearing chest pain to the back (Advanced)
item: While you transport, how do you treat the pressure?
content: Answer: Rate first (β-blocker toward ≈ 60), then a vasodilator for systolic ≈ 100–120. Other options: Vasodilator first, then a β-blocker | Leave it — the pressure is protective | Fluids to maintain perfusion of the false lumen. Explanation: Anti-impulse therapy lowers the force of each ejection (dP/dt) as well as the pressure. A vasodilator alone causes a reflex tachycardia that increases shear on the flap.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Type B dissection with a rising creatinine (Expert)
item: What is the new finding at the renal level?
content: Story: Known type B dissection on esmolol and nicardipine. Pain persists, urine output is falling. Step to the renal level of the CTA. Answer: The left kidney enhances poorly — its artery arises from the false lumen. Other options: Both kidneys are normal | A retroperitoneal haematoma | The flap has extended into the ascending aorta. Explanation: The branch fed by a poorly flowing false lumen is under-perfused: renal malperfusion.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Type B dissection with a rising creatinine (Expert)
content: Answer: It is now a complicated type B: urgent endovascular repair, not medical therapy alone. Other options: Nothing — continue anti-impulse therapy | It becomes a type A dissection | Stop the β-blocker to raise renal perfusion. Explanation: Malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain or uncontrolled hypertension turn an uncomplicated type B into a complicated one, which is treated by covering the entry tear.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Better after blood — then worse (Advanced)
item: How has she responded to blood?
content: Story: Grade IV splenic injury. After one litre of blood half an hour ago her heart rate had settled. It is climbing again and the FAST stripes are wider. Answer: Transient responder: she improved, then bled the blood away — still bleeding. Other options: Responder: stable, observe | Non-responder: no change at all | Over-transfused. Explanation: A transient response means ongoing haemorrhage at a rate the transfusion only briefly matched.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Better after blood — then worse (Advanced)
content: Answer: Haemorrhage control: embolisation if immediately available and safe, otherwise the operating room. Other options: Another litre of crystalloid and a repeat FAST in an hour | Observation on the ward | A CT of the head first. Explanation: Blood buys time; only stopping the bleeding fixes it. Unstable patients go to the operating room rather than the CT or angiography suite.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Severe pain, soft abdomen (Advanced)
content: Story: 78-year-old in atrial fibrillation, off anticoagulation, with an hour of severe central abdominal pain. The abdomen is soft. Lactate 1.4. The CT angiogram is on the screen at the renal level. Answer: The superior mesenteric artery does not fill: embolic occlusion. Other options: A normal CT — the pain is functional | An aortic dissection | Free air. Explanation: The SMA should be a bright dot in front of the aorta. An embolus from the left atrium has blocked it.

where: Abdomen › Challenge › Severe pain, soft abdomen (Advanced)
item: The lactate is normal. Is that reassuring?
content: Answer: No — lactate often stays normal until the bowel is infarcting. Other options: Yes — ischaemia always raises lactate early | Yes — it excludes infarction | Only if the pain improves. Explanation: Early ischaemia may not raise the systemic lactate. Pain out of proportion plus an embolic source needs urgent CT angiography and revascularisation.

where: Brain › Challenge › Sudden weakness and no words (Novice)
content: Story: Right-handed 67-year-old found by his wife an hour after last known well. Examine, then decide. Answer: Left middle cerebral artery (M1). Other options: Right middle cerebral artery | Basilar artery | Left posterior cerebral artery. Explanation: Right face, arm and leg weakness with global aphasia, gaze toward the left and a right field defect: the whole left MCA territory in a left-dominant patient — a proximal (M1) occlusion.

where: Brain › Challenge › Sudden weakness and no words (Novice)
content: Answer: CT with CT angiography (± perfusion) to confirm a large-vessel occlusion for thrombectomy. Other options: MRI before any decision | Wait for the deficit to settle — it may be a TIA | Lumbar puncture. Explanation: A severe cortical deficit predicts a large-vessel occlusion. Non-contrast CT excludes haemorrhage; CTA shows the clot; perfusion shows how much is still salvageable. Go to a thrombectomy-capable centre.

where: Brain › Challenge › Left weakness, talking normally (Intermediate)
content: Story: Right-handed 71-year-old, sudden left-sided weakness. She says she feels fine. Answer: Right middle cerebral artery (M1). Other options: Left middle cerebral artery | Right posterior cerebral artery | Basilar artery. Explanation: Left hemiparesis with gaze to the right, a left field defect and neglect of the left side: the right MCA territory.

where: Brain › Challenge › Left weakness, talking normally (Intermediate)
content: Answer: Language lives in the left (dominant) hemisphere; the right hemisphere gives neglect instead. Other options: The occlusion is too small | Aphasia appears only after 24 h | Aphasia is a brainstem sign. Explanation: In most right-handed people language is left-hemispheric. A non-dominant stroke can be as large but shows neglect and anosognosia — “she feels fine” is part of the deficit.

where: Brain › Challenge › Bumping into doorframes (Intermediate)
content: Story: 63-year-old keeps walking into things on her left. Strength and speech are normal. Answer: Right posterior cerebral artery — occipital cortex. Other options: Left posterior cerebral artery | Right middle cerebral artery | Left eye. Explanation: A left homonymous hemianopia (both eyes, left half of the field) comes from the right occipital cortex, supplied by the right PCA.

where: Brain › Challenge › Bumping into doorframes (Intermediate)
item: The NIHSS is low. What does that mean?
content: Answer: Posterior-circulation strokes score low; a low score does not mean a small or harmless stroke. Other options: It is too mild to image | It excludes a vascular cause | It means the stroke is in the brainstem. Explanation: The scale weights limb power and language. Visual, cerebellar and brainstem deficits are under-scored — judge the deficit, not the number.

where: Brain › Challenge › Dizzy, then unresponsive (Advanced)
content: Story: 55-year-old, vertigo and slurred speech this morning, now barely rousable with weakness of all four limbs. Answer: Basilar artery. Other options: Left middle cerebral artery | Both anterior cerebral arteries | Right internal carotid. Explanation: Reduced consciousness, gaze palsy, four-limb weakness, dysarthria and ataxia: the brainstem and cerebellum, supplied by the basilar artery.

where: Brain › Challenge › Dizzy, then unresponsive (Advanced)
content: Answer: Protect the airway, then emergent CTA and thrombectomy — the window is often wider for basilar occlusion. Other options: Supportive care only — prognosis is fixed | MRI first to confirm | Wait for a second opinion before imaging. Explanation: Untreated basilar occlusion is usually fatal or devastating. The airway is at risk from the depressed consciousness and bulbar weakness; reperfusion is offered later than for anterior strokes in many centres.

where: Brain › Challenge › A blown pupil after an ICH (Advanced)
content: Story: Left basal-ganglia haemorrhage, intubated for transfer. The haematoma has grown. Look at the pupils and the motor response. Answer: Left uncal herniation: the temporal lobe is compressing the left third nerve. Other options: Right uncal herniation | Tonsillar herniation | An eye drop was given. Explanation: The pupil on the side of the mass dilates and stops reacting first, as the uncus is pushed over the tentorial edge onto the third nerve.

where: Brain › Challenge › A blown pupil after an ICH (Advanced)
content: Answer: Head up 30°, hyperosmolar therapy, keep MAP up; brief hyperventilation only as a bridge. Other options: Prolonged hyperventilation to a PaCO₂ of 25 | Lower the blood pressure to a MAP of 60 | Lie the patient flat to improve cerebral blood flow. Explanation: Hypertonic saline or mannitol draws water out; head-up improves venous drainage. Hyperventilation lowers ICP by constricting vessels, which also cuts blood flow — minutes, not hours. CPP = MAP − ICP, so keep the MAP.

where: Brain › Challenge › Hypertension and bradycardia (Expert)
content: Story: Same patient, twenty minutes later. The pressure is climbing, the heart is slowing, and a colleague reaches for a vasodilator. Answer: The Cushing response — brainstem ischaemia from very high ICP. Other options: Autonomic dysreflexia | Pain — needs more analgesia | Hypertensive emergency causing the bleed. Explanation: High pressure, falling heart rate and irregular breathing: the brainstem is raising the MAP to force blood into a brain whose pressure is near arterial. It is a late, pre-terminal sign.

where: Brain › Challenge › Hypertension and bradycardia (Expert)
item: Should you drop the blood pressure?
content: Answer: No — the MAP is holding the CPP; treat the ICP (osmotherapy, surgery). Other options: Yes, to a systolic below 140 | Yes, with a vasodilator and a β-blocker | Yes, because bradycardia means the pressure is too high. Explanation: CPP = MAP − ICP. Lowering the MAP now drops cerebral perfusion further. The fix is to lower the ICP.

where: Brain › Challenge › The EVD suddenly drains fast (Expert)
content: Story: Left basal-ganglia haemorrhage with an EVD open at 15 cmH₂O. The nurse raised the head of the bed for transfer; now the drain is running quickly and the patient has a headache. Answer: The chamber was not moved with the head: it is now level with the ventricles, so it drains until pressure is near zero. Other options: The ICP has risen suddenly | The catheter is blocked | The transducer needs zeroing to air. Explanation: The drip chamber height is measured from the tragus (foramen of Monro). Raising the head lifted the ventricles to the chamber, removing the pressure the drain was set to hold. Over-drainage risks ventricular collapse and bleeding.

where: Brain › Challenge › The EVD suddenly drains fast (Expert)
content: Answer: Clamp briefly, re-level the zero to the tragus and reset the height, then reopen. Other options: Lower the chamber to drain even more | Leave it open — CSF drainage is always good | Flush the catheter. Explanation: Every position change needs the reference re-levelled. Many services clamp the drain for moves and re-level before reopening.

where: Heart › Challenge › An infant who sweats with feeds (Intermediate)
item: Which chambers carry the extra volume?
content: Story: Three-month-old, poor weight gain, breathless and sweaty with feeds. Watch the flow across the septum. Answer: Left atrium and left ventricle. Other options: Right atrium and right ventricle | Only the right ventricle | None — flow is balanced. Explanation: Blood crosses the VSD in systole straight into the pulmonary artery, goes round the lungs and returns to the LEFT atrium and ventricle, which dilate.

where: Heart › Challenge › An infant who sweats with feeds (Intermediate)
content: Answer: ≈ 2 : 1. Other options: 1 : 1 | ≈ 0.8 : 1 | ≈ 5 : 1. Explanation: The lungs receive about twice the systemic flow — pulmonary overcirculation, which is why the infant is breathless and fails to thrive.

where: Heart › Challenge › A big right heart (Intermediate)
content: Story: 34-year-old with exertional breathlessness; the echo shows a dilated right heart. Watch the atrial septum. Answer: Right atrium and right ventricle. Other options: Left atrium and left ventricle | Left ventricle only | None. Explanation: At atrial level the left atrium empties partly into the right, so the extra flow passes through the right atrium and right ventricle before the lungs.

where: Heart › Challenge › A big right heart (Intermediate)
item: Why is there little murmur from the defect itself?
content: Answer: The pressure difference between the atria is tiny, so the flow is low-velocity. Other options: The defect is closed in systole | The flow is right to left | Murmurs only come from valves. Explanation: Atrial pressures differ by only a few mmHg. The murmur heard is from the extra flow across the pulmonary valve, with fixed splitting of the second sound.

where: Heart › Challenge › Blue at thirty (Advanced)
content: Story: Adult with an unrepaired VSD, now cyanosed and breathless. The old murmur has gone. Answer: Pulmonary resistance has risen above systemic, so the shunt has reversed right to left. Other options: Heart failure has made the left ventricle leak | The defect has closed | Pneumonia. Explanation: Years of overcirculation remodel the pulmonary arterioles. Once PVR exceeds SVR, deoxygenated blood crosses into the systemic side: Eisenmenger syndrome.

where: Heart › Challenge › Blue at thirty (Advanced)
content: Answer: Only a little — shunted blood never meets the alveoli. Other options: Yes, fully | Oxygen makes it worse | Yes, after 20 minutes. Explanation: Oxygen corrects low-V/Q units but not true shunt. A little rise can come from pulmonary vasodilation; avoid systemic vasodilators, which increase the right-to-left flow.

where: Heart › Challenge › Stroke after lifting (Advanced)
content: Story: 29-year-old diver with a sudden aphasia after heavy lifting. Recent long-haul flight. Watch the atrial septum during the strain. Answer: Paradoxical embolism: straining raised right-atrial pressure above left and a venous clot crossed the PFO. Other options: An atrial septal defect with left-to-right flow | Carotid dissection from lifting | Air embolism from the dive only. Explanation: A PFO is a flap valve normally held shut by the higher left-atrial pressure. Valsalva, coughing or a PE reverse the gradient and open a path from the venous to the arterial side.

where: Heart › Challenge › Stroke after lifting (Advanced)
item: Why is the PFO silent at rest?
content: Answer: Left-atrial pressure keeps the flap closed; there is no flow until right pressure rises. Other options: It is too small to hear | Flow is continuous but low-velocity | It only opens during sleep. Explanation: No gradient, no flow: that is why bubble studies are done with a Valsalva release.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › High pressures after a central line (Novice)
content: Story: Ventilated trauma patient, new subclavian line. Peak pressures alarm, saturation and blood pressure fall. A film happened to be taken for line position. Answer: Right tension pneumothorax — pleural edge, no markings beyond it, flat hemidiaphragm, mediastinum pushed left. Other options: Right lung collapse from a plugged bronchus | Bilateral pulmonary oedema | A normal film. Explanation: Air outside the lung with the mediastinum pushed away and the hemidiaphragm flattened: pleural pressure is high.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › High pressures after a central line (Novice)
item: Next time this happens, what comes first?
content: Answer: Decompress on clinical grounds — do not wait for a film in an unstable patient. Other options: Always get a film first to confirm | Increase PEEP to re-expand the lung | Give a fluid bolus and reassess. Explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. The film here is a teaching picture; in practice needle or finger thoracostomy comes before imaging when the patient is crashing.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › No sliding on the right — needle? (Intermediate)
content: Story: Desaturation after turning; breath sounds absent on the right. Your colleague sees no sliding on the right and reaches for a needle. Tap each zone and watch the pleural line and M-mode. Answer: No — there is a lung pulse: the pleura still touch; the lung is collapsed, not separated. Other options: Yes — absent sliding means pneumothorax | Yes — the M-mode is a barcode | Cannot tell without an X-ray. Explanation: Absent sliding alone is not diagnostic. A lung pulse (pleural line twitching with the heartbeat) proves the visceral pleura is against the chest wall — here the right lung is airless from a plugged bronchus.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › No sliding on the right — needle? (Intermediate)
content: Answer: Clear the airway — suction, bronchoscopy, recruit — not a needle. Other options: Needle decompression | Chest drain | More PEEP only. Explanation: Needling a chest without a pneumothorax creates one. The problem is in the bronchus.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Asthmatic, high pressure, falling BP (Advanced)
content: Story: Intubated asthmatic. Peak pressures are high and the blood pressure is falling. Is it a pneumothorax? Scan all four zones. Answer: Sliding with A-lines in all four zones — pneumothorax very unlikely at these sites. Other options: Absent sliding on the right — pneumothorax | B-lines everywhere — oedema | A lung point on the left. Explanation: Sliding at the anterior chest excludes a pneumothorax under the probe with high certainty. The lungs are hyperinflated, not separated from the chest wall.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Asthmatic, high pressure, falling BP (Advanced)
item: What is the likely cause and first move?
content: Answer: Dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP): disconnect briefly to let the air out, then slow the rate. Other options: Needle both sides | Increase the rate to clear CO₂ | Fluid bolus and more PEEP. Explanation: Trapped gas raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return. A short disconnection lets it escape; then lengthen expiratory time.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Frothy secretions (Intermediate)
content: Story: 66-year-old intubated with pink frothy secretions after a large anterior MI. Answer: Cardiogenic oedema — perihilar opacity, septal lines, big heart, effusions. Other options: ARDS — peripheral patchy opacities with a normal heart | Tension pneumothorax | Hyperinflation. Explanation: A large heart, a central “bat-wing” distribution, septal (Kerley) lines and effusions point to raised left-atrial pressure.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Frothy secretions (Intermediate)
content: Answer: Many B-lines in both lungs, confluent in places, with effusions. Other options: A-lines everywhere | Absent sliding | A lung point. Explanation: Interstitial water turns the lung surface into vertical B-lines. They fall as the oedema clears — a quick bedside trend.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Pneumonia, worsening hypoxaemia (Advanced)
content: Story: 36-year-old with pneumonia, now P/F well below 150 on high FiO₂. Answer: Bilateral patchy opacities with air bronchograms and a normal heart — ARDS pattern. Other options: Cardiogenic oedema | Right lung collapse | Normal film. Explanation: Bilateral opacities not explained by effusion, collapse or heart failure, with a normal heart size, fit ARDS.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Pneumonia, worsening hypoxaemia (Advanced)
content: Answer: Tidal volume ≈ 6 mL/kg predicted body weight, plateau ≤ 30, PEEP to keep the lung open. Other options: 10 mL/kg to recruit the lung | Zero PEEP to protect the heart | High rate, low PEEP. Explanation: Lung-protective ventilation limits stretch of the small “baby lung” that remains aerated.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Desaturation after the move (Intermediate)
content: Story: Intubated at the scene. After moving to the aircraft stretcher the saturation falls and the peak pressure has risen. Breath sounds are quieter on the left. A film was taken on arrival. Answer: The tube tip is below the carina in the right main bronchus, and the left lung is collapsing. Other options: A left tension pneumothorax | A left pleural effusion | The tube is in the oesophagus. Explanation: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, so a tube pushed too far goes right. The left lung gets no ventilation and collapses as its gas is absorbed.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Desaturation after the move (Intermediate)
content: Answer: Deflate the cuff, withdraw the tube 1–2 cm, re-check depth and breath sounds, then recruit. Other options: Needle decompress the left chest | Increase the PEEP and FiO₂ only | Exchange the tube for a larger one. Explanation: Pulling the tip back above the carina re-opens the left main bronchus; the collapsed lung then needs a few breaths or a recruitment manoeuvre. Note the depth at the teeth.

where: Blood gas › Challenge › The laryngoscopy that takes too long (Intermediate)
item: How long before the saturation falls below 90 %?
content: Story: Three-month-old (6 kg), well pre-oxygenated and paralysed for intubation. Your colleague is still looking at the cords 75 seconds after the last breath. The saturation still reads high. Answer: Well under a minute — call time now and ventilate. Other options: About five more minutes | About eight minutes, as in an adult | It will stay up while it reads this high. Explanation: The reading is high because the top of the dissociation curve is flat, but the infant’s small oxygen store is nearly used up. Below 90 % the fall is fast.

where: Blood gas › Challenge › The laryngoscopy that takes too long (Intermediate)
item: Why is the infant so much faster than an adult?
content: Answer: Oxygen use per kilo is about twice as high, from a smaller lung volume that collapses after induction. Other options: Infants have less haemoglobin binding capacity at every age | Their pulse oximeters read late | They breathe faster, which uses up oxygen. Explanation: Oxygen consumption of ≈ 7–8 mL/kg/min drains a functional residual capacity that the soft infant chest lets fall to ≈ 15 mL/kg.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Barking cough, stridor (Novice)
item: By how much has the resistance to quiet breathing risen?
content: Story: Two-year-old with a barking cough and stridor at rest, frightened and starting to cry. The subglottis has about a millimetre of swelling all round. Answer: About 16 times. Other options: About 2 times | About 4 times | It has not changed. Explanation: Laminar resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius: from 4 mm to 2 mm diameter halves the radius, 2⁴ = 16.

where: Ventilator › Challenge › Barking cough, stridor (Novice)
content: Answer: Upsetting the child — crying makes flow turbulent and the work of breathing much higher. Other options: Letting the parent hold the child | Sitting the child up | Giving humidified oxygen by a mask the child tolerates. Explanation: Turbulent flow through the narrowed segment needs pressure that rises with the fifth power of the radius (× 32). Keep the child calm and upright, with a parent.

where: Lines › Challenge › A quiet, pale four-year-old (Intermediate)
content: Story: Four-year-old (16 kg) hit by a car 40 minutes ago. Quiet, pale and cool. The arterial line is in. Her blood pressure is reassuring, says a colleague. Answer: Yes — compensated shock: tachycardia, narrow pulse pressure, cool skin with a normal pressure. Other options: No — the systolic pressure is normal for her age | Only if the capillary refill exceeds 6 s | Not until she becomes hypotensive. Explanation: Children maintain their pressure with tachycardia and intense vasoconstriction until about a third of their blood volume is lost. Hypotension is late.

where: Lines › Challenge › A quiet, pale four-year-old (Intermediate)
item: What if her heart rate starts to fall without treatment?
content: Answer: Pre-arrest: the failing, hypoxic heart is slowing — act now. Other options: She is improving | Pain relief is working | Normal for sleep. Explanation: In a shocked child bradycardia is an ominous sign that the heart is running out of oxygen.

where: Heart › Challenge › Pink hand, blue feet (Advanced)
item: What does the difference between the probes tell you?
content: Story: Term newborn, meconium at delivery, now four hours old and hard to oxygenate. Two probes: right hand and a foot. Answer: Right-to-left flow across the ductus: pulmonary pressure is at or above systemic — PPHN. Other options: A faulty foot probe | Normal newborn transition | Left-to-right flow through a PDA. Explanation: The ductus enters the aorta beyond the right subclavian artery. Deoxygenated blood crossing it reaches the legs, not the right hand.

where: Heart › Challenge › Pink hand, blue feet (Advanced)
item: Which of these lowers pulmonary resistance?
content: Answer: Oxygen, normal CO₂, warmth, correcting acidosis — and inhaled nitric oxide. Other options: Letting the CO₂ rise to protect the lungs | Keeping the baby cool | Restricting oxygen to avoid toxicity. Explanation: Hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis and cold all constrict the pulmonary vessels. Inhaled nitric oxide relaxes pulmonary vessels selectively.

where: Heart › Challenge › Both probes low, no difference (Expert)
content: Story: Same baby a few hours later. The right hand and the foot now read the same — and both are low. A colleague says the difference has gone, so the PPHN is better. Answer: No — blood is now also crossing the foramen ovale right-to-left, lowering both hand and foot. Other options: Yes — no difference means no pulmonary hypertension | Yes — the ductus has closed, so the problem is solved | The probes must both be faulty. Explanation: Shunting at atrial level mixes deoxygenated blood before the aorta, so pre- and post-ductal saturations fall together. A low pre-ductal saturation still needs an explanation.

where: Heart › Challenge › Both probes low, no difference (Expert)
item: What raised the right atrial pressure?
content: Answer: A struggling right ventricle pumping against high pulmonary resistance. Other options: Too much oxygen | Closure of the ductus arteriosus by itself | Low pulmonary resistance. Explanation: Against a high pulmonary resistance the right ventricle dilates and its filling pressure rises until right atrial pressure exceeds left and the flap opens.

where: Blood gas › Challenge › Emergency intubation at 38 weeks (Advanced)
content: Story: Rapid-sequence induction at term for eclamptic seizures. Pre-oxygenated well. Four minutes into a difficult laryngoscopy the saturation is still high. Answer: Stop and oxygenate now (mask or supraglottic airway): she is about a minute from the cliff. Other options: Keep going — 98 % leaves plenty of time | Wait for the saturation to reach 90 % before stopping | Apply cricoid pressure harder and continue. Explanation: A smaller functional residual capacity and higher oxygen use give a term pregnancy about five minutes, not eight — and the fall below 90 % is steep.

where: Blood gas › Challenge › Emergency intubation at 38 weeks (Advanced)
item: What would have bought her more time?
content: Answer: Head-up position during pre-oxygenation and nasal oxygen during the attempt. Other options: Lying her completely flat | Pre-oxygenating with room air | Hyperventilating after induction. Explanation: Head-up (with left uterine displacement) gives back some lung volume; oxygen flowing through the nose keeps topping up the alveoli during apnoea.

where: Lines › Challenge › Faint on the stretcher at 36 weeks (Novice)
item: What is the most likely cause?
content: Story: 36 weeks pregnant, transferred for reduced fetal movements. Lying flat on the stretcher she becomes pale, sweaty and light-headed. Answer: Aortocaval compression: the uterus is squeezing the inferior vena cava. Other options: Hidden haemorrhage | Pulmonary embolism | Vasovagal fainting only. Explanation: Supine at term, venous return falls and output drops by up to a third; the low CVP fits.

where: Lines › Challenge › Faint on the stretcher at 36 weeks (Novice)
content: Answer: Left uterine displacement — tilt her or push the uterus to the left. Other options: A 2 L fluid bolus | Start a vasopressor infusion | Raise her legs while keeping her flat. Explanation: Relieving the compression restores venous return within a minute; the placenta, which has no autoregulation, benefits at once.

where: Lines › Challenge › Bleeding after delivery, pressure “fine” (Advanced)
content: Story: Thirty minutes after a vaginal delivery, a soft uterus and ongoing bleeding. The estimated loss is nearly two litres. The midwife says the blood pressure is fine. Answer: Very — the shock index is well above 1: she is compensating for a large loss. Other options: Not very — the systolic pressure is still near 90 | Only if she becomes confused | Only once the pressure falls below 70. Explanation: Pregnant women hold their pressure until late because of a 6.5 L blood volume and strong vasoconstriction. Heart rate divided by systolic pressure unmasks the loss.

where: Lines › Challenge › Bleeding after delivery, pressure “fine” (Advanced)
content: Answer: Uterine massage and uterotonics, tranexamic acid, blood and products, call for help. Other options: Crystalloid until the pressure is normal, then reassess | Wait for a haemoglobin result | Vasopressor to raise the pressure. Explanation: Treat the cause (uterine atony is the commonest) and replace blood; early tranexamic acid reduces death from bleeding.

where: Lines › Challenge › The BP that nobody believes
item: What is the most likely problem?
content: The arterial line reads about 135/73 and the trace looks spiky. The cuff just read about 115/78. The patient looks well. Answer: Underdamped line — resonance from a small bubble or long tubing. Other options: Overdamped line — a clot at the tip | The transducer is too low | True hypertension — the cuff is wrong. Explanation: A systolic overshoot with a normal MAP and a ringing square-wave test is underdamping. Do a fast-flush test (more than 2 oscillations), find the bubble, aspirate and flush.

where: Lines › Challenge › CVP 25 after the chest X-ray
content: The bed was sat up to 30° for a chest X-ray. Since then the CVP reads about 25 and the MAP has risen 20 mmHg. Nothing else has changed and the patient looks the same. Answer: The phlebostatic axis rose but the transducer did not — it now sits below the axis. Other options: Fluid overload from the X-ray contrast | The transducer drifted — it needs zeroing | Tension pneumothorax. Explanation: Both lines rose by the same amount at the same moment: a reference-level error. Sitting the patient up raised the axis about 27 cm, so every reading is ≈ 20 mmHg too high. Re-level the transducer to the axis.

where: Lines › Challenge › Flat line after the blood gas
content: Two minutes after an arterial blood gas was drawn, the monitor alarms: ART reads 0 with a flat trace. The patient is talking to you. Answer: The sampling stopcock was left open to air. Other options: Cardiac arrest | Massive clot in the radial artery | The pressure bag burst. Explanation: A flat line at zero in a talking patient is a system problem. The sampling port was left open to air with the stopcock off to the patient, so the transducer reads atmosphere. Cap it, turn the stopcock back to the patient, and check for blood loss. (Had it been left open toward the patient, blood would run out — or, on a central line, air would be drawn in.)

where: Lines › Challenge › Blunted and getting worse
content: The arterial trace has lost its dicrotic notch and looks rounded. Systolic has drifted down to about 110. Drawing blood back from the sampling port is sluggish. Answer: Overdamped: a clot at the catheter tip. Other options: Underdamped: long tubing | Hypovolaemia | Aortic stenosis. Explanation: Rounded trace, lost notch, low systolic, high diastolic, MAP unchanged, and a square-wave test with no bounce: overdamped. Sluggish blood return points to a clot. Aspirate it — never flush a clot forward into the radial artery.

where: Lines › Challenge › Hypotension that isn’t
content: After the transducer was changed, the arterial line reads 26/−21 with a perfect-looking waveform. The patient is pink and talking; the cuff reads about 115/78. Answer: It was zeroed while open to the patient. Other options: The transducer is 60 cm too high | Severe vasodilatory shock | The line is overdamped. Explanation: The shape is normal but the whole waveform is shifted down by about the patient’s own mean pressure. Zeroing with the stopcock open to the patient made the monitor treat the MAP as “zero”. Turn the stopcock off to the patient, open to air, zero, and turn it back.

where: Lines › Challenge › Blood in the tubing
content: Blood has crept up the arterial tubing toward the transducer and the trace is becoming damped. The fast-flush only reaches about 90 mmHg. Answer: Pressure bag under-inflated — below arterial systolic. Other options: Transducer below the axis | Catheter in the vein | Underdamped system. Explanation: The flush bag must be at 300 mmHg — above systolic — or blood backs up the line, the continuous flush stops and the catheter clots. Inflate the bag to 300 and flush the blood back.

where: Lines › Challenge › The CVP that pulses to 25
content: The CVP trace now swings from about 2 to 25 mmHg with every beat, and there are occasional ectopic beats. Freeze the monitor and look at the shape. Answer: The catheter tip has migrated into the right ventricle. Other options: Giant v waves from tricuspid regurgitation | Cannon a waves from heart block | An underdamped CVP line. Explanation: A sharp systolic rise to ≈ 25 and a diastolic floor near zero is a ventricular trace. TR can give a large c-v wave, but diastolic pressure stays high. Notify the provider and get a chest X-ray; stop vasoactive infusions through that lumen until the tip is confirmed. The provider withdraws it to the cavo-atrial junction; ectopy settles once the tip leaves the RV.

where: Lines › Challenge › Onto the transport stretcher
item: Before changing the norepinephrine, what do you suspect?
content: You have just moved the patient onto the transport stretcher. The arterial trace looks smudged and MAP reads higher than a minute ago. Norepinephrine 0.1 µg/kg/min is running. Find everything that is wrong before you touch the pump. Answer: A monitoring problem: the transducer was not re-levelled and the trace is damped. Other options: The septic shock has resolved | The norepinephrine dose is too high | Fluid overload. Explanation: A sudden change after moving a patient is a monitoring problem until proven otherwise. The transducer stayed at the old bed height (reading high), and the wrist is flexed, kinking the cannula (damped). Level, straighten the wrist, check with a flush test — then titrate to the real MAP.

where: Lines › Challenge › Six hours after cardiac surgery
content: Six hours after valve surgery, the chest drains have stopped draining. Heart rate about 130. Look at both traces with the breathing. Answer: Cardiac tamponade. Other options: Hypovolaemia from bleeding | LV failure | Complete heart block. Explanation: High CVP (≈ 18) with no y descent, a narrow pulse pressure, and systolic falling more than 10 mmHg on each breath in (pulsus paradoxus): tamponade. Hypovolaemia would have a low CVP. Treatment: surgical re-exploration or pericardiocentesis.

where: Lines › Challenge › Slow and strange
item: What causes the tall CVP waves?
content: Heart rate 38. Every so often a very tall wave appears on the CVP trace. Answer: Cannon a waves: atria contracting against a closed tricuspid (AV dissociation). Other options: Giant v waves of tricuspid regurgitation | Catheter in the right ventricle | Artefact from coughing. Explanation: The tall waves are intermittent and fall where an independent P wave lands during ventricular systole: cannon a waves of complete heart block. The slow rate also gives large stroke volumes and a wide pulse pressure.

where: Lines › Challenge › A bounding pulse
content: The arterial trace shows a steep upstroke, a very low diastolic pressure and no clear dicrotic notch. Answer: Aortic regurgitation. Other options: Aortic stenosis | Hypovolaemia | Tamponade. Explanation: Very wide pulse pressure, low diastolic pressure, steep upstroke and a lost notch (often a bisferiens double peak): aortic regurgitation. AS is the opposite — slow, small and late.

where: Lines › Challenge › Slow to rise
content: An elderly patient with a systolic murmur. The arterial upstroke is slow, with a shoulder on the way up, and peaks late. Answer: Aortic stenosis. Other options: Aortic regurgitation | Septic shock | Stiff arteries only. Explanation: Pulsus parvus et tardus — a small, late, slow-rising pulse with an anacrotic shoulder — is aortic stenosis.

where: Lines › Challenge › Is she fluid-responsive?
item: What do you make of the PPV?
content: Ventilated, MAP 80. The monitor shows a pulse-pressure variation over 30 %. The team suggests a fluid bolus. Answer: It cannot be used: the rhythm is irregular (AF). Other options: Over 13 % — give fluid | Over 13 % — start a vasopressor | It proves she is overloaded. Explanation: PPV needs a regular rhythm: in AF every beat has a different filling time, so the pulse pressure varies whatever the volume status. Use a passive leg raise or a fluid challenge with a cardiac-output measure instead.

where: Lines › Challenge › Resuscitate the bleeding patient
item: Is this patient likely to respond to fluid?
content: Haemorrhage, now controlled. Ventilated at 8 mL/kg, sinus tachycardia. Use the waveform to guide fluid. Answer: Yes — PPV > 13 % on controlled ventilation in sinus rhythm. Other options: No — the CVP is low | Cannot tell without a cuff pressure | No — the MAP is 65. Explanation: All the conditions for PPV are met and it is well above 13 %. Give fluid in 500 mL steps and re-check the variation after each.

where: Lines › Challenge › Warm, vasodilated and hypotensive
item: What does the waveform suggest is the main problem?
content: Septic shock after 2 L of fluid. MAP in the high 50s, low diastolic, low dicrotic notch. Answer: Low vascular tone — a vasopressor is needed. Other options: Pump failure — start an inotrope | Severe hypovolaemia only | Tamponade. Explanation: Low diastolic pressure with a notch near the diastolic level and a high heart rate: vasoplegia. Norepinephrine restores tone. PPV is still just above 13 %, so some fluid may help alongside it.

item: Left pneumothorax — film taken in expiration — teaching points
content: Breathing out shrinks the lung but not the trapped pleural air, so a small pneumothorax is easier to see — expiratory films are not routine; an ordinary inspiratory film shows most. · Upright, pleural air rises to the apex; supine, it collects in front and at the base (the deep sulcus sign) instead. · Follow the markings to where they stop — skin folds, the scapula edge and external wires make lines too, but lung markings continue past them. · Tension is a clinical diagnosis — a crashing patient gets decompressed, not a film. Here the mediastinum is central.

item: IVC — long axis under the liver — teaching points
content: Prove it is the IVC by following it into the right atrium — the aorta lies deeper and to the left and never enters the heart. · Measure 1–2 cm below the hepatic-vein junction, at right angles to the vessel. · Small and collapsing fits a low right-atrial pressure; wide and fixed fits a high one. · It does not reliably predict who will respond to fluid: positive-pressure ventilation, raised abdominal pressure, RV failure, tricuspid regurgitation and vigorous breathing all change it. · Read it with the lungs, the heart, the patient and the trend — never alone.

item: Internal jugular vein — long axis and collapse point — teaching points
content: In long axis both vessels are tubes, so shape cannot separate them — use depth, compressibility and pulsatility, and check in short axis too. · Doppler colour shows direction relative to the probe, not artery or vein: red and blue alone prove nothing. · Veins can look pulsatile from transmitted pulsation; an artery still will not collapse. · Where the vein sits over the artery, a needle through both walls of the vein reaches the carotid — keep the tip in view. · The collapse point moves with volume and breathing: head-down tilt or a Valsalva fills the vein and gives a bigger target.
